items.title: I asked AI if it was OK to use AI to write an obituary. The answer surprised me | Anna Spargo-Ryan
items.summary:
Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel

I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her.

The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum, by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done.

Continue reading...
items.t: I asked AI if it was OK to use AI to write an obituary. The answer surprised me | Anna Spargo-Ryan

items.title: ‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults
items.summary:
Lancet survey shows under-45s have sex twice a month – down from four times in 1990 – and one in three under-25s have never had intercourse

Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse.

The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, found the average adult under 45 now has sex twice a month, continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving. 

She never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office. 

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

The two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil. 

Three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

Aren’t we all at least a little bit tired all the time? So when should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? But if you’ve been struggling night after night to fall asleep, you can’t seem to stay asleep, or you never feel well-rested in the mornings , it might be a sign that your sleep needs a little TLC. And yes, even if you’re hesitant to take medications to help you fall and stay asleep , there are actually other treatment options you can try.

Scary Mommy spoke with Dr. Jessica Meers , board-certified sleep psychologist and founder of Rhythm Wellness Sleep Solutions, to find out where you should turn for insomnia help first — and what treatment options even exist.

When should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? When does “I’m struggling to fall asleep lately” become “I should really see my doctor about this”?

“If it feels like a problem to you, it’s worth having a conversation about,” says Meers. Whether you’re overly tired during the daytime, feel like you can’t sleep long or well enough, or just unhappy with your sleep in one way or another, that’s reason enough to ask for help, she says.

And how do you know if you really have insomnia? Is there a line where sleep troubles become clinical?

items.title: School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray
items.summary:
In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school. 

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day? 

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

What are the School Nutrition Standards? 

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by…
items.t: School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

items.title: I Travel With A Kid Who Has Severe Allergies. Here Are The Things I Never Thought To Worry About

A hotel room that looks clean could be holding fragrances that trigger respiratory symptoms. The swimming pool down the hall could pose problemsThat gluten-free item on the menu during our family night out could be cross-contaminated. As a parent, I’ve learned that keeping my son safe means thinking beyond the obvious risks.

With the colder weather settling in and holiday travel approaching, I knew it was time to take a closer look at what families like mine should be considering before hitting the road or boarding a plane. So, I chatted with experts Dr. Sarah Beebe, a travel advisor and autism travel professional based in Lewes, Delaware, and Dr. Tracy Tyson, a pediatrician with 20 years experience in urgent care, who helped me identify the less obvious triggers families might encounter while traveling—and how to better prepare for them.

The Allergic Kid Through the colder months and when planning trips, I’d always assumed that keeping my son’s inhaler on hand was enough. But a recent hospital stay made me realize his asthma is far more severe than we’d understood, and that I needed to take a more proactive approach to managing it.

I researched all of the common triggers, such as dust, pet dander, pollen, smoke and weather changes. After chatting with Dr. Tyson and Dr. Beebe, I learned of the lesser-known hazards that can lurk in the places we stay and the ways we travel.

A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

items.title: Tim Dowling: there’s been a break-in, and I have to remove the culprit
items.summary:
Finding a rat relaxing in my late father-in-law’s cottage is unnerving. As always, my wife takes command of the situation

In the year since my father-in-law died my wife and I have visited his cottage, on average, every other week – more often in spring and summer. In theory, this is often enough to keep abreast of appointments with people coming to deal with various issues: slipped roof slates, fallen trees, electrical problems. In practice, more can go wrong than gets put right in the interval.

This time we’ve been away for three weeks. My son was meant to go down, but his plans changed. We need to be there to meet someone measuring up for two replacement windows, and whatever else.

items.title: “Financially, I Regret Having My Third Child” & 61 Other Anonymous Mom Confessions
items.summary:
Natalia Lebedinskaia/Getty Images As we barrel towards December, money is top of mind for a lot of moms. And, really, that makes sense any year: the holidays are expensive . As moms, we’re always doing the math in our heads: how much we can afford, how much we need to cut, how much is going out vs. how much is coming in. And this year, a lot of moms are finding that the math just ain’t mathing . That theme kept surfacing in this week’s roundup of anonymous confessions. 

One mom wants a divorce but says that, in this economy, it isn’t possible. Another admits that, financially, she regrets having her third child. One mom got laid off and one mom is tired of working her ass off yet always feeling broke, and one mom, in her own words, just wants to be left alone with a lot of money. 

The cost of everything is dictating a lot right now, and moms are really feeling that. 

Then there are the other confessions that showed up this week, the kind that bubble up every week. Worries about being a good parent. Health concerns. Perimenopause ( always perimenopause !). Little wins that moms need to share with someone. 

So, here are this week’s confessions, shared anonymously by moms yelling into the void about everything from money to marriage. 

Scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram . And to browse past Confessions, take a look here .
items.t: “Financially, I Regret Having My Third Child” & 61 Other Anonymous Mom Confessions

items.title: 9 Frozen Puff Pastry Desserts That Only Look High Effort
items.summary:
There are few kitchen shortcuts I love more than keeping a box of puff pastry in the freezer. It’s the secret weapon behind so many desserts that look like they came from a fancy bakery, even when you barely had to lift a finger to make them. We’re talking flaky layers, pretty little twists, golden-brown pastries and impressive-looking tarts, all without the hassle of cutting cold butter into flour while simultaneously pouring in ice water (IYKYK).

Whether you’re hosting a holiday party, need something to bring to a cookie exchange, or just want to make a weekend dessert at home feel a little more special, these recipes deliver plenty of wow factor thanks to a box of frozen puff pastry.

1. Nutella Puff Pastry Twists A Sweet Thyme If Nutella is your love language, these Nutella puff pastries from A Sweet Thyme need to be on your baking list. Store-bought puff pastry gets brushed with melted butter, spread with Nutella, and sprinkled with ground hazelnuts before being folded, sliced, and twisted into pretty little pastries. They bake up golden and flaky in just 12 to 15 minutes, making them look like something you’d pick up at a European bakery.

2. Churro Twists Princess Pinky Girl You don’t need a deep fryer or a trip to your favorite churro stand to get that cinnamon-sugar goodness. Princess Pinky Girl ’s churro twists use just three ingredients — puff pastry, melted butter, and cinnamon sugar — to bring this dream dessert to the table. The whole recipe takes about 15 minutes, which means you can have a batch ready before your guests even finish their first cup of…
items.t: 9 Frozen Puff Pastry Desserts That Only Look High Effort
